skills.when_to_use: Use when the question demands precise cross-video correspondence, discrimination, or selection among videos/options, recognizable from the question text and video list alone: questions that reference labeled object IDs across synchronized camera views and ask where one object is when an event involving another occurs, or ask about a labeled object's trajectory, final motion, position in a frame, or visibility; questions that name a time interval or timestamp in one video and ask for the functionally equivalent step or interval in another, or otherwise require a time-interval answer about a specific visible action; questions asking which of several videos, segments, or options exhibits a stated property, state, error, or ending condition; or questions asking which action is performed incorrectly a stated number of times across videos of the same activity. Do not use for open narrative inference questions (e.g., predicting a middle segment from a beginning and an ending) where summarizing each video separately suffices.
skills.strategy:
Apply this procedure in order; it overrides the default single-pass workflow.

Stage 1, first acquisition. If the question references labeled object IDs in synchronized camera views (each label appears only briefly at the object's first visible second), begin with one joint watch of the referenced views rather than per-video analyses: separate whole-video passes routinely miss the brief labeled window and return null. Ask the visual model to locate each referenced ID from its labeled first-appearance window, then give a timestamped, purely descriptive account of the referenced objects' and any named reference object's positions and movements, with no verdict about which option is correct. For every other question type (equivalent-step intervals, property or error selection among videos, counts of incorrect actions), issue one per-video instruction per referenced video asking for a timestamped, purely descriptive account: every occurrence of the target action across the whole video, each with visible start and end seconds and visible attributes. Do not embed answer options, a yes/no verdict request, or an expected conclusion in the first pass. For property-selection questions, ask each video for raw descriptions of the relevant moments (who and what is present, positions, objects held, visible threats or errors) and decide the property yourself from those raw details, never from an analyst's verdict. For a referenced event at a stated time, request that interval plus several seconds of surrounding context.

Stage 2, consistency gate before answering. Compare all accumulated reports against each other, the required output format, and the answer options. You must not answer while any flag is open: (a) two reports about the same object or moment directly conflict, including a later report locating something an earlier report called not visible; (b) a null report (a referenced object or event reported not visible or unidentifiable) that would make the question unanswerable; (c) degenerate evidence, such as a single point timestamp where an interval with distinct start and end is required, an action with no visible duration, or an event or interval anchored at exactly 0.0 seconds or at a selected clip's boundary, which often reflects the label window or clip edge rather than the true event; (d) a report whose raw visual description contradicts its own interpretive conclusion; (e) a candidate interval or time obtained from a watch whose total selected duration was long relative to the detail sought, so sampling was too sparse to localize a brief action; (f) a raw observation that matches none of the answer options. A null report from a sparse or separate pass is not evidence that the object is absent, stationary, or out of view.

Stage 3, mandatory targeted re-acquisition. For each open flag, run the matching follow-up before answering, within the available decision steps. For a referenced labeled ID reported not visible: run one dense joint watch of the views clipped to the first several seconds (the labeled window) and, if a specific moment is asked about, a tight window around that moment; ask for the labeled boxes and the raw visual layout. For identity or position conflicts, or an off-option observation: run one joint watch of the relevant videos clipped to a short window around the claimed moment, keeping total selected duration small so sampling stays dense; ask for the raw visual layout of the labeled objects without stating which option is correct; if the re-observed position still matches no option, re-read all raw descriptions for a detail that resolves the choice rather than reinterpreting the observation through speculation about which view or framing the question implicitly means. For boundary-anchored events: densely re-watch the first several seconds and any later candidate moments before accepting them. For any time-interval answer: before submitting it, run one dense confirmation watch on a tight window covering the candidate interval plus a few seconds before and after, asking for the action's full visible start and end seconds, how long it visibly continues, and whether the same action occurs at any other time; adjust or reject the candidate interval according to this confirmation rather than the original sparser pass.

Stage 4, final answer from raw description. Answer only from described visual content, not from an analyst's or visual model's verdict phrase and not from plausibility priors about intended answers. Match the requested output format exactly, including the numeric style of any given example (e.g., plain integer seconds when the example uses them). If the question presupposes exactly one correct option but all raw descriptions still fail to support any option, do not select an option merely through guesswork: choose the option whose support rests on the strongest described visual details, re-read the raw descriptions for a resolving detail, and record the residual uncertainty in the answer's reason. Never map a null report onto an option such as 'stays in place' or 'not visible' without the dense joint confirmation of Stage 3, and never substitute a discussion of missing evidence for the requested answer representation.
